INSURANCE ACCESSIBILITY BY FARMERS OF REMOTE AREAS

2752. SHRI AMARSING TISSO:

Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE be pleased to state:

(a) the number of farmers in Karbi Anglong and Dima Hasao districts covered under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana;

(b) whether the Government has identified any issues in coverage or claim settlement in these remote regions; and

(c) the steps taken to improve insurance accessibility for small and marginal farmers in these districts?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE AND

FARMERS WELFARE (SHRI RAM NATH THAKUR):

(a) Total 30,950 and 72,011 farmer applications have been enrolled during last 5 years i.e. 2020-21 to 2024-25 in Dima Hasao and Karbi Anglong districts of Assam respectively under Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY).

(b) The PMFBY, introduced in the country from Kharif 2016 season is voluntary16.12.2025 961 for the States as well as farmers. All the major work like selection of crops and area/district, selection of insurance model, selection of Insurance Companies through transparent bidding process, enrollment of farmers, assessment of crop yield/crop loss and uploading of Threshold Yield and Actual Yield on National Crop Insurance Portal (NCIP) for calculation and payment of admissible claims directly to the farmer's account are being performed by the concerned State Government or Joint Committee of State Government officials and insurance company concerned. The roles and responsibilities of each stakeholder are defined in the Operational Guidelines of the scheme for the proper execution of the scheme.

(c) Government has taken various steps to strengthen implementation of this scheme all over India including Assam State to bring transparency and ensure smooth coverage farmers and timely settlement of claims in States/UTs :

• Government has undertaken development of National Crop Insurance Portal (NCIP) as a single source of data ensuring subsidy payment, co-ordination, transparency, dissemination of information and delivery of services including direct online enrollment of farmers, uploading/obtaining individual insured famer's details for better monitoring and to ensure transfer of claim amount electronically to the individual farmer's Bank Account.

• In order to rigorously monitor claim disbursal process, a dedicated module namely 'Digiclaim Module' has been operationalized for payment of claims from Kharif 2022 onwards. It involves integration of16.12.2025 962 NCIP with Public Finance Management System (PFMS) and accounting system of Insurance Companies to provide timely and transparent processing of all claims.

• Delinking of Central Government share of premium subsidy from that of State Governments has been implemented so that farmers can get proportionate claims relating to the Central Government share.

• As per the Operational Guidelines of PMFBY, in case payment is not made timely by Insurance Company, a penalty of 12% is auto- calculated and levied through National Crop Insurance Portal (NCIP) w.e.f. Kharif 2024.

• Similarly, if State Government delayed its premium subsidy from stipulated time period, a penalty of 12% is to be paid by them also.

• Tranche based claims payment has been initiated from 2025-26.

• Also, towards leveraging technology in implementation of the scheme, various steps like capturing of yield data/Crop Cutting Experiments (CCEs) data through CCE-Agri App and uploading it on the NCIP, allowing insurance companies to witness the conduct of CCEs, integration of State land records with NCIP, introduction of technologies like YES-TECH (Yield Estimation System Based on Technology) and WINDS (Weather Information Network and Data System) for objective crop damage and loss assessment etc. have already been taken to improve timely settlement of the claims to farmers.

• The Government has actively supported the awareness activities being16.12.2025 963 carried out by the States concerned including Assam, implementing Insurance Companies, financial institutions, and Common Service Centres (CSCs) network to disseminate key features of PMFBY amongst farmers and members of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs).

• Structured awareness campaign 'Crop Insurance Week/Fasal Bima Saptah' has been initiated by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare since Kharif 2021 season onwards. Along with this, 'Fasal Bima Pathshalas' are also being organized at village/GP level for knowledge building of farmers on various aspects of scheme implementation.

• Government had also organized a nationwide Doorstep Crop Insurance Policy/receipt Distribution mega drive – 'Meri Policy Mere Haath'. Hard copies of crop insurance policy receipts are distributed to farmers enrolled under PMFBY through special camps at gram Panchayat/village level.

SUPPORT TO FARMERS AFFECTED BY CLIMATE-RELATED EVENTS

2753. SHRI E. T. MOHAMMED BASHEER:

Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS' WELFARE be pleased to state:

(a) the details of the relief and support which have been extended to farmers affected by climate-related events in 2025; and

(b) the details of the progress made with respect to the Pradhan Mantri Fasal16.12.2025 964 Bima Yojana (PMFBY) (crop insurance) and the Minimum Support Price (MSP) policies?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE AND

FARMERS WELFARE (SHRI RAM NATH THAKUR):

(a) As per the National Policy on Disaster Management (NPDM), the primary responsibility for disaster management, including disbursal of relief assistance to the affected, rests with the State Government concerned. State Governments undertake relief measures in the wake of natural calamities, from the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) already placed at their disposal as per approved norms. Additional financial assistance is provided from the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF), in case of disaster of 'severe nature'. Details of the fund allocated and released under SDRF/NDRF to the States are available on website i.e. ndmindia.mha.gov.in.

(b) Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) provides comprehensive risk coverage against crop damage from pre-sowing to post-harvest for cereals, millets and pulses or oilseeds, and commercial or horticultural crops notified by concerned State Government. The scheme safeguards against widespread yield loss due to natural risks such as flood, inundation, landslide, drought, dry spells, hailstorm, cyclone, pests/diseases, natural fire/lightning, storm, typhoon, tempest, hurricane, and tornado. It also provides coverage against farm-level yield loss due to localized risks (hailstorm, landslide, inundation, cloudburst, and natural fire) and post-harvest losses due to cyclone, unseasonal rain, and hailstorm. As of 30.11.2025, ₹1, 90,374 crore has been disbursed as claims to16.12.2025 965 approximately 2,301 lakh farmers since inception of the Scheme in Kharif 2016.

Government declares Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for 22 mandated crops, 14 Kharif, 6 Rabi, and 2 commercial crops (jute and copra), based on the recommendations of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) and in consultation with State Governments and Central Ministries. While fixing MSP, factors such as cost of production, demand–supply trends, domestic and international prices, inter-crop price parity, and terms of trade are taken into account. MSP ensures a minimum margin of 50% over the cost of production to the farmers. The increase in MSP has significantly benefited farmers, as reflected in the steady rise in procurement levels and MSP payments made.

From 2014–15 to 2025–26 (up to October 2025), 117.32 crore metric tonnes of crops have been procured, with MSP payments of ₹24.49 lakh crore. The details of MSPs fixed by Government for the year 2025 are given in the enclosed Statement.

2756. SHRI PRADYUT BORDOLOI:

Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to

state:

(a) whether the Government provides incentives and subsidies to the domestic tea producers of the country, if so, the details thereof along with the categories and criteria for providing such incentives;

16.12.2025 973

(b) whether the Government plans to establish a minimum sustainable price per KG of produced tea and/or green leaves, if so, the details thereof along with the rate of minimum sustainable price for tea and the rationale behind its determination, if not, the reasonstherefor including regarding the reasoning behind not expanding minimum sustainable price to tea;

(c) whether the Government plans to shift tea from the ambit of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry to the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' welfare, if so, the details thereof including the reasoning behind not expanding minimum sustainable price to tea; and

(d) whether the Government plans to provide subsidies for setting up mini- factories exclusively for the small tea growers, if so, the details thereof, if not, the reasons therefor?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND

INDUSTRY; AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF

ELECTRONICS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (SHRI JITIN

PRASADA):

(a) Tea Board is implementing the 'Tea Development and Promotion Scheme (TDPS)' across the country. Under the scheme, the Tea Board provides support to tea growers for various activities, which inter alia include replantation of old and senile tea bushes, raising of tea nurseries, support for organic certification and conversion, mobilization of small growers into Self Help Groups (SHGs)/ Farmers Producer Organizations (FPOs) and conducting trainings and capacity- building workshops for improving production, productivity, and quality of tea produced in the country. The modalities and guidelines of the TDPS scheme are16.12.2025 974 available on Tea Board's website at https://teaboard.gov.in/pdf/Letter_to_ stakeholders_03_10_2024_combined_pdf8764.pdf.

(b) Presently, no such proposal is under consideration. However, in order to ensure fair price realization to the tea growers especially the small growers, Tea Board had introduced Price Sharing Formula (PSF) for fair sharing of sale proceeds between the grower and the manufacturer in a certain ratio based on the cost of production of green leaf and made tea. Further, in order to ensure proper implementation of PSF, prices for green leaf are fixed based on average auction price and notified for each tea district and payment of green leaf price to the growers is monitored by the District Green Leaf Price Monitoring Committees headed by the District Magistrates.

(c) Presently, no such proposal is under consideration of this department. (d) Under Tea Development and Promotion Scheme, Tea Board provides financial assistance for setting up of mini tea factories by SHGs/FPOs. Financial assistance is provided at the rate of 40% of the actual cost incurred on machinery and civil works, subject to a ceiling limit of Rs 33.00 lakhs per factory (excluding land cost). In case of SC/ ST applicants, financial assistance is provided at the rate of 50% of the actual cost incurred on machinery and civil works, subject to ceiling limit of Rs 50.00 lakhs per factory (excluding land cost).

IMPLEMENTATION OF MGNREGS IN ANDHRA PRADESH

2757. SHRI DAGGUMALLA PRASADA RAO:

SHRI LAVU SRI KRISHNA DEVARAYALU:

Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

16.12.2025 975

(a) the details of the total number of funds allocated, released and disbursed under Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) during the last five years for Andhra Pradesh, year and district-wise;

(b) the details and the total number of days of employment provided during the last five years in Andhra Pradesh, year and district-wise;

(c) the work demand under MGNREGS during the last five years in Andhra Pradesh, district and year-wise; and

(d) the details of the total pending liabilities (wage and material) and number of people impacted during the last five years in Andhra Pradesh, year and district-wise?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT

(SHRI KAMLESH PASWAN):

(a) Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (Mahatma Gandhi NREGS) is a demand driven wage employment scheme.

There is no State/UT-wise allocation of funds under Mahatma Gandhi NREGS.

Details of funds released to the State of Andhra Pradesh under Mahatma Gandhi NREGS in the last five financial years from FY 2020-21 to 2024-25 are given below:

Financial Years 2024-25 2023-24 2022-23 2021-22 2020-21
Central fund released to the State of Andhra Pradesh (Rs. in crore) 7,707.21 7,353.67 8,008.81 7,195.81 10,306.30
16.12.2025 976

While wage payments are directly credited by Central Government to the account of beneficiaries through the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) protocol, for material component, funds are released to the State Government, which in turn releases the funds to Districts through SNA SPARSH module.

(b) District-wise details of persondays generated in the State of Andhra Pradesh under Mahatma Gandhi NREGS during the last five financial years are given in the enclosed Statement-I.

(c) District-wise details of households demanded work in the State of Andhra Pradesh under Mahatma Gandhi NREGS during the last five financial years are given in the enclosed Statement -II.

(d) As on 10.12.2025, the total pending liabilities of Wage payment in respect of State of Andhra Pradesh are Rs. 413.72 crore and an amount of Rs. 573.62 crore is pending liability for Material component.

District-wise details of the number of workers who availed the employment in the State of Andhra Pradesh under Mahatma Gandhi NREGS during the last five financial years are given in the enclosed Statement -III.

AUTOMOTIVE MISSION PLAN 2047

2760. SHRI KHAGEN MURMU:

Will the Minister of HEAVY INDUSTRIES be pleased to state:

(a) the current status of the formulation of the Automotive Mission Plan (AMP) 2047, including the progress made by the seven sub-committees tasked with developing milestones for 2030, 2037 and 2047;

(b) whether the Government has identified the key thematic areas or priority domains that will guide the AMP 2047 roadmap;

(c) if so, the details thereof;

(d) whether any preliminary assessments have been undertaken regarding the challenges facing the automotive sector; and

(e) if so, the manner in which these challenges are proposed to be addressed under AMP2047?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEAVY INDUSTRIES; AND

MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI BHUPATHI RAJU

SRINIVASA VARMA):

(a) to (e) Automotive Mission Plan 2047 is an industry-led initiative aimed at making the Indian automotive industry globally competitive. It seeks to integrate16.12.2025 984 the collective vision of stakeholders, including OEMs, auto component manufacturers, policymakers, academia, and end users, to address challenges like technological advancements and charging infrastructure. The meetings of seven Sub-Committees are convening periodically and priority domains, assessments and challenges will be addressed in Automotive Mission Plan.

SHRI N.K.PREMACHANDRAN (KOLLAM): Sir, I rise to oppose the introduction of the Bill, the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Bill, 2025.

The first objection is regarding the title of the Bill, namely, the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Bill, 2025. Previously, so many amendments of the insurance laws have come to this House, and this is an Insurance Laws (Amendment) Bill. There is a specific provision in the legislative process. Kaul & Shakdher is very specific that the title of the Bill should convey the message regarding the intent and content of the Bill which has to be explicitly given to the public or given to the people at large. So, the title should be clear enough while being drafted. But it is quite unfortunate.

I would like to quote Kaul & Shakdher Page No. 587:

"Every Bill has a title succinctly describing the nature of the proposed measure. Care is taken to see that the title is sufficiently wide to cover all the provisions of the Bill, and that it is not vague, for, otherwise it may invite amendments outside the scope of the proposed measure".

16.12.2025 1020

So, this is very clear. Now, coming to this Insurance Laws Bill, what is the relation of the 'Insurance Laws' with the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha? So, the title of the Bill has nothing to do with the contents of the Bill.

Now, I come to the contents of the Bill. Is 100 per cent FDI in the Life Insurance Corporation as well as in any insurance sector helping the poor people and the marginalized section of the society? So, 100 per cent FDI in the insurance sector is adversely affecting national interest. I have not got much time because merits are not to be discussed.

Another provision is regarding the commission of the Life Insurance Corporation agents and other insurance agents which will be determined by the Insurance Regulatory Development Authority of India according to the new provision. In the original Bill, it was to be decided by the Parliament and as per the rules and regulations made by the Parliament. But it is quite unfortunate to note that the Insurance Regulatory Development Authority of India is given the authority to describe and determine the commission of the LIC agents.

Even now, it is very well known to all, as several times I have also raised the issue of the LIC agents in the House, their commission has drastically reduced and thereby the number of LIC agents have come down like anything.

The LIC agents are the backbone of the Life Insurance Corporation. But unfortunately, they have not been taken care of. In such a situation, the new Bill is not for insurance of the common people. It is not for the suraksha of the common people and the ordinary people. Therefore, I strongly object to it.

Another objection of mine is also there. I would like to seek a ruling. I16.12.2025 1021 would like to raise a point of order also in this regard. My point of order is in respect of Article 348 of the Constitution of India. I would like to have a ruling on this. I raise a point of order under Article 348 of the Constitution of India and the relevant provisions of the India's Official Languages Act of 1963. I seek your kind ruling on this important Constitutional aspect relating to the language in which the Bills are being drafted and introduced in Parliament. … (Interruptions) I want a ruling. A specific ruling is required. … (Interruptions) Sir, this point of order is not political in nature please. It goes to the constitutional validity, legislative discipline and legal certainty of parliamentary legislation.

Article 348 of the Constitution clearly provides that the authoritative text of the Bills to be introduced in either House of the Parliament and all of Acts passed by the Parliament shall be in English language, unless Parliament by law otherwise provides. This Constitutional mandate remains unchanged and binding on this House.

object to the introduction of the Bill on three grounds in pursuance of Rule 72 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.

Amendment of Section 2C of the Bill to provide foreign Insurance16.12.2025 1023 companies an ultimate say in insurance business in India is against the sovereignty, unity and integrity of nation, and is a violation of constitutional provisions.

Amendment of section 2CA of the Bill, the insertion of clause (a) and (b) is against the interest of the national insurance companies as, it shall not apply to an insurer or insurance intermediary in any Special Economic Zone including International Financial Services Centres, set up under the provisions of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005. It shall apply to the insurer or insurance intermediary in any Special Economic Zone including International Financial Services Centres, set up under the provisions of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, with such exceptions, modifications and adaptations as may be specified in the notification to facilitate 100 per cent foreign players in the insurance sector.

This is my objection. This is untenable and unjustifiable as it is against the Indian insurance sector.

In view of the above objections, I respectfully submit that the Bill is liable to be rejected at the very threshold, being beyond the jurisdiction of Parliament and violative of the Constitution of India.

PROF. SOUGATA RAY: Sir, under Rule 72(1) of the Rules of Procedure, I oppose the introduction of the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Bill, 2025. This is another example of Hindi-isation of legislation in this country. You give the name of the Bill in such a manner that Hindi becomes the 'introduction', and then Government slogans are incorporated into16.12.2025 1024 the Bill. यह जो 'सबक(cid:236) बीमा, सबक(cid:236) सुर(cid:177)ा' है, यह सब गवन(cid:170)म(cid:164)ट का (cid:214) लोगन है । यह िबल का ल(cid:167)(cid:181) वेज नह(cid:233) होना चािहए ।

Lastly, I want to say that in the insurance sector, we are actually working backwards. Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru nationalised the life insurance sector in 1956. Shrimati Indira Gandhi nationalised the general insurance sector in 1972.

Now, we are moving in the reverse direction. Slowly, IRDA was set up in 1999, and now hundred per cent FDI in the insurance sector is being allowed. This is going to favour the corporates and not the common people and common insurers.

The rural population is still outside the ambit of insurance. I think this is a superfluous Bill. This is a backward-looking Bill, and, that is why, I oppose its introduction.

SHRI T. M. SELVAGANAPATHI (SALEM): Sir, this is the problem. This is exactly the core of the problem, where you name all your schemes, Acts and statutory measures in Hindi. This is the difficulty which we are facing now.

Sir, we oppose even the very name of the Bill – Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Bill, 2025. This Bill amends the Insurance Act, the LIC Act and the IRDA Act. I do not want to repeat what our learned friends Shri Premachandran, Dr. T. Sumathy and Prof. Sougata Ray have already stated.

Fundamentally, ours is a welfare State, where the Constitution, through its Directive Principles, directs the State to provide social security and healthcare to its citizens. Article 41 clearly says:

16.12.2025 1025

"The State shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement...."

This particular Bill completely dismantles this welfare aspect of our Constitution. Take, for example, the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948. It is a statutory welfare legislation that mandates the Government to provide medical care to insured persons and their families, cash benefits during sickness, maternity and employment injury, as well as funeral and dependent benefits.

I would like to impress upon this Government that it should be rolling out more such welfare-oriented Bills, because State-backed social security for workers such as Accredited Social Health Activists, Anganwadi workers, under the Mahatma Gandhi National Employment Guarantee scheme, which is now going to be renamed RAM, auto-rickshaw drivers, taxi drivers, tailors, the under- privileged and the poor will be directly hit because of hundred per cent foreign investment. Therefore, we strongly object to the introduction of this Bill. It should be withdrawn.

DR. SHASHI THAROOR (THIRUVANANTHAPURAM): Thank you, Mr.

Speaker, I would also like to oppose the introduction of the proposed Bill, The Viksit Bharat – G Ram G Bill, which represents a deeply regrettable and retrograde step for our nation and our nation's commitment to the welfare of its most vulnerable citizens.

My first objection, Mr. Speaker, as with others, is the ill-advised decision to remove the name of the father of the nation, for the reasons already given, which I will not repeat. This is not just an administrative tweak; it is an assault on the very spirit and philosophical foundation of this crucial programme.

Mahatma Gandhi's vision of Ram Rajya was never a purely political programme. It was a socio-economic blueprint rooted in the empowerment of villages, and his unwavering faith in Gram Swaraj was part of his vision of Ram Rajya. So, the original Act, by bearing his name, acknowledged his profound conviction that true employment guarantee and upliftment must flow from the grassroots, embodying his principle of "the last man first".

To remove the name of Mahatma Gandhi is to strip the Bill of its moral compass and its historical legitimacy, and then to have two languages in the title, merely to make the acronym "G RAM G", is not just a violation of Article 348, as pointed out in the previous discussion, but it also reminds me of a song, of a lyric16.12.2025 1037 from my childhood.

हम लोग बचपन म(cid:164) गाते थे-

देखो ऐ दीवान(cid:332) तुम ये काम न करो,

राम का नाम बदनाम न करो ।

We must also seriously question the legislative intent behind the financial restructuring proposed in the Bill. The proposal to impose 40 per cent of the financial burden directly on the State Governments is not just fiscally irresponsible, but it is a measure that threatens to make the entire programme unviable.

This sudden and massive shift in liability will inevitably make it impossible for poorer States. It will lead to delays in wage payments, reduced days of work, and ultimately the destruction of the Scheme itself. It is a violation of fiscal federalism, which is why I do not think we have the legislative competence to do that.

Finally, it also makes the scheme contingent upon executive notification, allowing the Union to decide when and where the scheme will operate. This fundamentally alters the ratio of the programme.

(ii) Need to include algorithmic accountability and platform liability under proposed Digital India Act

SHRI MUKESHKUMAR CHANDRAKAANT DALAL (SURAT): AI is next

generation technology of the world. India is also rapidly advancing in AI positioning itself as a new player globally. World's largest tech giants are looking towards India to invest billions of dollars into AI & cloud infrastructure in India.

India's "India AI Mission" has Rs 10371.92 cr. funding to boost AI ecosystem.

India plans to have contribution of $1 trillion in its economy by 2035. AI adoption is surging in defence, telecommunication, electronics, healthcare, agriculture,16.12.2025 1046 education & fintech. Since AI is relatively a newer concept in India, it is yet framing AI policies, rules and regulations on data protection, safety, ethics & mitigating deepfakes. Of all these deepfakes are biggest concern & threats to the country, particularly for youth, women, & political leaders & reputed citizens of the country. These AI-generated fake videos/audio can mislead people, damage reputation, & spread distress, disgust & distrust in the country. India's Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) at present tracks deepfake cases. India's IT rules 2021 mandate platforms to remove deepfake cases in India. Yet, I suggest that to safeguard people against misuse of AI, the Government needs to draft still stricter laws under Digital India Act & create awareness among people about AI. I suggest that the Digital India Act may include AI-specific clauses addressing algorithmic accountability & platform liability.

(iv) Need to transfer major Railway Stations presently under the Banaras division to Sonepur division and restoration of sections currently under Muzaffarpur division to Sonepur division

SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY (SARAN): At present several key sections of my Saran Parliamentary Constituency such as Chhapra, Masrakh, and Kaptaganj fall under the Banaras Division of the North Eastern Railway (NER), causing significant operational and administrative inconvenience. Simultaneously, the Sonepur Railway Division of the East Central Railway (ECR) is facing a continuous erosion of its jurisdiction and revenue base. Important stations and sections have been repeatedly transferred, and the recent exclusion of the Muzaffarpur–Karpurigram section from Sonepur to the Samastipur Division has further weakened Sonpur's operational control and financial stability. This fragmentation has disrupted planning, infrastructure development, and passenger services. I therefore propose that major stations presently under the Banaras Division (NER) transferred to the Sonepur Division of the ECR, and that sections shifted to Muzaffarpur Division be restored to Sonepur division. This realignment will enhance administrative convenience, improve operational efficiency, and ensure a fair and balanced distribution of revenue.

(xii) Need to grant fast-track project status to the Purna-Akola doubling of rail line project in Maharashtra

SHRI ANUP SANJAY DHOTRE (AKOLA): I would like to request the Hon'ble Railway Minister to address the need for doubling the Purna–Akola railway line, a long-pending section crucial for ensuring seamless movement from the South to the North-West. This pre-Independence railway corridor historically connected the princely state of Rajasthan (including Jaipur) to the Deccan region and continues to hold strategic and economic significance. The doubling of this route is essential to decongest traffic, enhance operational efficiency, and support the increasing passenger and freight movement in the region. Therefore, I urge the Hon'ble Minister to grant fast-track project status to the Purna–Akola track-doubling work at the earliest.

(xvii) Need for establishment of medical and nursing colleges in Meghalaya

SHRI SALENG A. SANGMA (TURA): I would like to bring it to the notice of Hon'ble Minister of Health and Family Welfare regarding shortage of specialist doctors, nurses and other technical staff in the state of Meghalaya. Therefore, if Government could take steps to establish two medical colleges and two more nursing colleges alongwith technical institution relating to health in the State, the health related problems being faced by the people could be addressed.

(xviii) Need to declare Mahatma Basaveshwara Jayanti as a National event and include his ideals in school curriculum in the country SHRI SURESH KUMAR SHETKAR (ZAHIRABAD): I wish to draw the attention of the Government to the urgent need for national recognition of Mahatma Basaveshwara, a visionary 12th-century philosopher and social reformer. His revolutionary ideals of social justice and gender equality, challenging caste discrimination centuries ago, are foundational to the spirit of our Constitution.

16.12.2025 1056

Mahatma Basaveshwara established the Anubhava Mantapa, often referred to as the world's first spiritual Parliament—a truly democratic platform open to all sections of society, predating institutions like Magna Carta. His principles of "Kayakaive Kailasa" (Work is Worship) and "Dasoha" (Service and Equal Distribution) remain relevant guiding principles for building a fair society today.

While Mahatma Basaveshwara Jayanti is celebrated in several states, his universal message warrants national recognition. I humbly request the Central Government to officially declare Mahatma Basaveshwara Jayanti as a formal National Event across the country. Furthermore, I urge the Ministry of Education to include Mahatma Basavanna's inspiring biography, his message of equality, social harmony, and democratic values in national school textbooks (NCERT/CBSE) to educate our youth and reaffirm India's proud civilizational truth that "India is the Mother of Democracy."

(xxi) Need for direct flight connectivity between Kolkata and European countries

SHRI YUSUF PATHAN (BAHARAMPUR): West Bengal is one of the most favoured tourist destinations in the country with the state witnessing the 2nd highest foreign tourist footfall in India in 2025. Despite this huge foreign interest in the state, there are no direct flights connecting Kolkata to Europe. This deprives Bengal of both revenue and economic opportunities. Similarly, with over 2.5 lakh passengers travelling from Kolkata to Europe each year, the lack of direct flights imposes heavy costs in terms of time, money and convenience on students, businesspeople and tourists. Multiple MPs have, in the past,16.12.2025 1058 petitioned the Ministry of Civil Aviation for improving the connectivity between Kolkata and Europe. In December 2024, the West Bengal State Assembly passed a unanimous resolution seeking the Union Government's intervention to ensure direct flights between Kolkata and Europe. West Bengal's strategic location will also ensure that direct flight connectivity from Kolkata to Europe will cater not just to the whole Eastern and Northeastern India but also to neighbouring countries like Bhutan, Nepal and Bangladesh. Hence, I urge the government to take speedy action to ensure that direct flight connectivity between Kolkata and Europe is established at the earliest.

(xxii) Need to provide financial assistance to set up a dedicated Cancer Hospital or District Cancer Centre in Ranipet district of Tamil Nadu SHRI S. JAGATHRATCHAKAN (ARAKKONAM): I would like to draw the urgent attention of the Government to the alarming increase in cancer cases in Ranipet district of my Parliamentary Constituency of Arakkonam, Tamil Nadu.

Tamil Nadu Government conducted the screening camps in Ranipet which examined more than 9,500 people, and hundreds of cancer cases—including detection of early-stage breast cancer. These numbers reflect a serious and growing public health challenge. However, Ranipet district does not have a dedicated cancer hospital or district cancer centre. Patients—many of them daily-wage earners—are forced to travel long distances to Chennai or Vellore for diagnosis, chemotherapy and radiotherapy. This delays treatment, increases out-of-pocket expenses, and causes immense hardship for families already struggling with the emotional and financial burden of cancer. I, therefore, request16.12.2025 1059 the Honourable Minister of Health and Family Welfare to sanction a dedicated Cancer Hospital or District Cancer Centre in Ranipet under central assistance, and to link it with the National Oncology Grid for technical support. This will bring timely, life-saving care within the reach of thousands of people. I urge the Ministry to take this matter on priority and order an immediate assessment of feasibility.

(xxiii) Need to set up an additional Kendriya Vidyalaya in Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh

SHRI BASTIPATI NAGARAJU (KURNOOL): At present, 37 Kendriya Vidyalaya's (KVs) are functioning in the State of Andhra Pradesh and Kurnool district has only one KV. During the academic year 2024–25, enrolment in the lone KV increased by nearly 12%, reaching 809 students, indicating growing demand and pressure on existing infrastructure. Kendriya Vidyalayas play a crucial role in providing quality education, particularly to the children of Central Government employees. With a district population of 22.71 lakh, the current number of KVs in Kurnool is clearly inadequate to meet educational needs.

Further, although the Central Government has approved 85 new KVs nationwide, including 8 in Andhra Pradesh, none has been sanctioned for Kurnool district. In view of the rising enrolment, population size, and the strategic importance of equitable access to Central Government schools, I request the Government to sanction additional Kendriya Vidyalaya's for Kurnool district at the earliest.

SHRI TANGELLA UDAY SRINIVAS (KAKINADA): I would like to seek the urgent intervention of the Union Government for the timely completion of critical infrastructure works at Rangaraya Medical College, Kakinada. During my recent inspection of the college, I reviewed the ongoing construction of the PG and UG hostels. I found that only 35% of the PG Ladies Hostel (G+4) and 15% of the PG Male Hostel (G+3) have been completed. The primary reason for this delay is the slow disbursement of sanctioned funds. As per the Detailed Project Report, the Central share is ₹33.12 crore, yet only ₹8.28 crore has been released so far, leaving essential works stalled and directly affecting postgraduate training and student facilities. India is expanding health infrastructure nationwide. In Andhra Pradesh, the NDA Government advances with holistic development. I urge the Centre to release pending funds for RMC to strengthen medical education in the Godavari region.

(xxviii) Need for early screening and preventive care programmes to address the threat posed by Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) in the country

SHRI SUNIL DATTATREY TATKARE (RAIGAD): Chronic kidney disease (CKD) occurs when the kidneys have become damaged over time. Globally, it is the ninth leading cause of death. CKD also increases the risk of other health problems like heart disease and stroke. Over the past 20 years, Chronic Kidney Disease has become a significant cause of concern for Indians. It has become among the top 10 risk factors in both men and women and also among the top16.12.2025 1063 10 causes contributing to total years of life lost, even more than diabetes. By some estimates, over 13 crore Indians are affected by the condition. Many cases likely go unreported, particularly in tribal areas. This disease is also known to contribute to a range of cardiovascular problems. In Maharashtra, the number of CKD cases over the past three years has been comparable to the number of cases of stroke. This disease is very preventable and manageable. Through proper preventive care and early detection, the burden can be brought down.

The Government is implementing early screening and preventive care programs for various diseases. I request that a similar approach be adopted for Chronic Kidney Disease under the Prime Minister's vision for a healthy and viksit Bharat.

ADV. DEAN KURIAKOSE (IDUKKI): Respected Sir, I stand here today to participate in what has become an annual ritual of this Government – the great legislative illusion, known as the Repealing and Amending Bill, 2025.…

(Interruptions)

Sir, the Government is painting a picture that it is reforming and cleaning up the Statute Book. They speak of 'Minimum Government, Maximum16.12.2025 1067 Governance'. They tell the nation that by passing this Bill, they are liberating us from the burden of history. But let us be honest about what is happening here today. This House, the highest forum of our democracy, is being made to spend its precious time – the time that belongs to the suffering farmers of our nation, the time that belongs to the unemployed youth of our nation, the time that belongs to the victims of climate disasters, etc. – on deleting laws that the same Government passed barely 24 months ago.

Sir, look at the First Schedule in this Bill. They are repealing the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 and also the Cinematograph (Amendment) Act, 2023. What kind of governance is this? In 2023, they celebrated these laws as 'historic reforms'. In 2025, they are repealing them to clean up the books.

What kind of drama is this? Is this Parliament a content creation factory for their PR team? Do we pass laws so that they can repeal them later and boast, 'Look, we removed 100 laws today'? This is not reform. It is a shameful thing. This is inflation of data. The Government must listen to it. You are padding your report card because you have no real achievements to show on the subjects that matter – jobs, economy, and social harmony. The confusion does not end there. You have thrown the entire criminal justice system into chaos by replacing the IPC and the Indian Evidence Act with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam respectively. Yet today, you have brought amendments to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. I would urge the Government to make up its mind. Are we in the 'Amrit Kaal' of new laws or are we still patching up laws passed during the colonial era? This Bill is a symbol of a Government that loves16.12.2025 1068 paperwork but hates accountability.

While you are busy fixing spelling mistakes in the Statute Book, the people of the country are facing many serious issues. The people of my constituency are facing many issues like human-animal conflict, natural calamities, etc. You have time to fix registered posts versus speed posts. But you have no time to fix the broken disaster compensation system. I refuse to appreciate this housekeeping exercise while the house itself is on fire. However, since we are forced to debate this Bill, let me expose the dangerous changes hidden inside this so-called routine legislation.

I would also like to express my strong concerns, reservations, and opposition to the Repealing and Amending Bill, 2025, introduced by the hon. Minister. While the Government claims that this is a routine housekeeping exercise to remove obsolete laws, a closer look at the Second Schedule reveals amendments that are not merely formal but have serious substantive implications for the common man and for our disaster resilience. How can we casually and lightly pass these amendments without any detailed discussion?

That is a major question.

Let me raise some concerns, limited only due to lack of time. The first concern relates to the dilution of clause 4, Second Schedule of the Disaster Management Act. I represent Idukki, a constituency highly vulnerable to natural calamities. The Disaster Management Act is very important for my constituency.

I am deeply concerned about the amendment proposed to the Disaster Management Act. The Bill seeks to amend Section 30, sub-Section 2, clause 6,16.12.2025 1069 replacing the word 'prevention' with 'preparation'. Both prevention and preparation are important for disaster management. Prevention is aimed at stopping a natural calamity whereas preparation is about getting ready for rescue works. Therefore, both are very important. But in this case, the word 'prevention' is being replaced with 'preparation'. I do not know what the relevance of this change is.

The Statement of Objects and Reasons claims that this rectifies an inadvertent error but we know that words matter in law. Prevention is a priority duty to stop disasters before they occur. Preparation means merely getting ready for the inevitable. By changing disaster management plans from prevention to preparation, are we signalling that the State is giving up on preventing ecological disasters? It is a serious question. In the context of climate change, we need stronger preventive measures and binding preventive mandates, not a semantic delusion that lowers the bar for district authorities. We cannot reduce our guard from prevention to mere preparation. The disaster management authorities of our country are doing both. However, the Government is diluting prevention and taking up preparation only. There is a serious lacuna.

Secondly, I oppose the amendments to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

First of all, the Government has to clarify whether it is amending the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 or the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. What is the sanctity of this process, when you do these activities again and again with no prior homework. The Bill seeks to replace the time-tested 'registered post,16.12.2025 1070 acknowledgement due' with 'speed post with registration and proof of delivery' in multiple sections, including Order 5 and Order 21.

Sir, 'acknowledgement due' requires a physical signature, a tangible proof that the specific individual has received the summons. 'Proof of delivery' in the Speed Post system is often just an online status update or a digital entry by a delivery agent. In rural India, where internet connectivity is still limited and digital literacy is evolving, relying solely on a system where a delivery agent marks an article as 'delivered' without a physical 'acknowledgement due' card is dangerous.

How will a poor litigant prove that he never received the summons, if the online system shows it as 'delivered'? This amendment removes the bracketed protection of 'registered post acknowledgement due' in Order 5, Rule 9, Clause 4, potentially weakening the verification process for defendants residing outside jurisdiction.

Sir, we are prioritizing speed over justice. This change is premature for rural India and the falsehood of repealing recent Acts (First Schedule). Finally, look at the First Schedule. The Government is repealing Acts as recent as 2023, such as the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 and the Cinematograph (Amendment) Act, 2023. While I understand the concept of spent laws, this annual ritual of passing Bills just to repeal amendments made last year is a waste of Parliament's time. It creates an illusion of reform boasting about repealing hundreds of laws, when you are simply deleting the Amendment Acts passed months ago.

16.12.2025 1071

Sir, I am concluding. I cannot support a Bill that simply dilutes our disaster management framework and jeopardizes the legal rights of rural litigants under the guise of modernisation.

I urge the Minister to withdraw the amendments to the Disaster Management Act and the Code of Civil Procedure very immediately because the Government is not at all taking it serious - while introducing this Bill - and is passing these kind of amendments without a detailed discussion. It is a dangerous thing also. I am opposing this Bill. Thank you very much.

Hon. Member, Dr. Kalanidhi Veeraswamy ji

DR. KALANIDHI VEERASWAMY (CHENNAI NORTH): Sir, thank you very much for giving me an opportunity to speak on the Repealing and Amending Bill, 2025.

We feel that the passing of this Bill is not at all necessary. You feel that you have a majority, and you are bringing in Bills, and you are either abrogating them or amending them according to your choices just because you have a majority.

I would like to speak about the great Mavalankar. He had spoken about how the minority should be treated. He said, "Just because you have a majority in the Parliament, by raising of hands, if you are going to vote on the sentiments of the people, this is not a country which is democratic." This is what he had mentioned. This Government is proving his words exactly right.

If you look at the Bills which have been brought, passed, and enacted as law, you will find that in the last 10 years, there have been several Bills which have been enacted and made as laws. The former Supreme Court Chief Justice, Mr. Ramana had mentioned, "We are not passing Bills with adequate debate, discussions, deliberations, or referring them to Standing Committees, and because of that, they are having problems in interpreting the law and passing judgments." Also we find that when you pass certain laws, within a year or two, you bring it back and again amend it. So, if you can amend one particular law, it should stand the test of time, where at least for a decade or two, it should be16.12.2025 1078 alive. But you are bringing in amendments, which are again re-amended and re- amended within a couple of years, showing that this Government does not have a clue about the direction in which they are travelling.

Sir, to talk about the laws which have been brought in, they are against the people, anti-democracy and anti-people. The farm laws are a one standing example. When you brought in the farm laws, Opposition Members, having discussed with the farmers, had brought out the farmers' sentiments, talking about not needing this particular Bill where it will destroy the farming community.

But just because you had a majority, you spearheaded yourself, and you made sure that it will be brought in by brute force. And there were thousands, if not lakhs of farmers, who had to protest, not for one day or two days, but for almost one and a half years, where 700 farmers had to die before you could realise their requirements and their requests, and then you had to repeal that.

Even when demonetisation was brought in, the hon. Prime Minister said that he will eradicate terrorism, he will eradicate counterfeit money and black money. He had mentioned all these things. He said that tie me to a post and whip me if this is not done within 90 days. Now, it has been been several years, and what was the effect of demonetisation? About 99.3 per cent of the notes have come back. So, where is the black money? You were talking about black money being hoarded all over the country, but we find that only the BJP people were having the Rs. 2000 notes. When it came out, the BJP people were the ones who had access to that and it was caught by the Income Tax Department, whereas the common man was standing in a queue and hundreds of people16.12.2025 1079 died standing in the queue.

These are the things that the Government has been doing. You had brought in abrogation of Article 370. When the abrogation of Article 370 was brought in, we were speaking against that because we felt that J&K needs do have a special place. It is a jewel of our country, bordering Pakistan. They had to have their own security. You said that you have removed it, and now, there will be no terrorist activities happening over there. But sadly, Pahalgam was a total failure of the intelligence of the Union Government's policing mechanism and their military activities. It is a blatant failure of this Government where five terrorists were able to come, not one or two kilometres, but hundreds of kilometres deep into the heart of India from Pakistan and kill about 27 tourists.

In response to that, when we wanted to have a negotiation, unilaterally you decided to go for a war. We did not know what was the objective of that war. We did not know what was the ultimate aim of that war. The only question we asked was, 27 people were murdered by terrorists, what happened to those five terrorists. None of them spoke about that.

HON. CHAIRPERSON : Please speak on the Bill.

DR. KALANIDHI VEERASWAMY: After the abrogation of Article 370, this is what has happened. So, I am talking about bringing in repeals, amendments and all these things. Anyway, you are doing it on your own, just because you have a brute majority.

I request the Union Government to at least listen to the Opposition and have discussions and deliberations. Even now, you are bringing in some laws16.12.2025 1080 whose names we cannot understand. Today, we are even changing the name of a Bill whose name I was not even able to pronounce. I am not even able to understand these words.

So, I request the Government to ensure that when they are bringing in a Bill, they make it in English, so that the whole country can understand it, and that you do not try to push Hindi down our throats by saying that these are the names of Bills and we have to say those names.

With these words, I oppose this Bill and hope that the Union Government will take cognisance of these words. Thank you.

SHRI SRIBHARAT MATHUKUMILLI (VISAKHAPATNAM): Thank you, Sir. I

rise to stand in support of the Repealing and Amending Bill, 2025, which addresses a subject that lies at the very heart of effective governance and is also very close to my heart. This is not optional; this is essential for a modern and dynamic democracy.

Some of my colleagues in the Opposition who have spoken here have raised certain points, which I will address later in my speech. But one thing on which I believe we can all agree, is that change is the only constant. Our Constitution-makers recognised this timeless truth. They understood that governance must evolve with society and, therefore, built Article 368 as the constitutional engine for reform. They did not give us a static document; they gave us a living Constitution – a framework that entrusts future generations with the responsibility to amend, repeal, and refine laws as India progresses.

Over the decades, however, our legislative system has developed serious16.12.2025 1081 structural imbalances. I have personally experienced this in many aspects of my life, where governments are very good at adding laws, adding rules, and adding conditions, but are very poor at removing or updating outdated ones. This unnecessary burden is faced by everyone – from the common man to the poorest of the poor, and even by the highly wealthy.

Every new policy brings with it fresh compliance requirements, new penalties, and additional layers of regulation. Rarely do we pause to ask whether old provisions have outlived their relevance or whether they now contradict newer laws. The result is regulatory congestion, which burdens citizens, businesses, and Government officers alike, creating confusion and discretionary enforcement. We have seen how some bad actors misuse this discretion to harm the interests of citizens and even the nation. I am happy to note that the current NDA Government has taken concrete steps over the last decade to relieve citizens and businesses of this burden.

More than 40,000 unnecessary compliances have been abolished, easing procedural hurdles and reducing red tape. Over 1,500 outdated and redundant laws have been repealed, clearing the statute book of colonial-era provisions and laws that no longer serve India's development.

I would like to point out a few things here. Some Members of the Opposition have said that we are changing laws within three years or four years.

We must recognise that we are living in the era of artificial intelligence and quantum computing, where the world is changing rapidly, and we have to keep adapting.

16.12.2025 1082

One must also reflect on the approach we adopt: whether we wait endlessly for perfection or ensure that we are good enough to move forward, while continuing to amend and improve as we go along. If I had to choose between perfection and being good enough to move forward, I would always choose being good enough because we should not be trapped in policy paralysis.

This is important to highlight because during the UPA regime between 2004 and 2014, only a single repeal Bill was introduced, which repealed just two outdated laws. This starkly contrasts the approach of the current NDA Government with that of the earlier UPA regime, which largely neglected the task of revising and repealing obsolete laws.

Sir, I am an active Member of the Select Committee on the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Bill,2025 and I have been participating actively in rationalising penal provisions and simplifying compliance, with the objective of improving ease of living and ease of doing business. I hope that the same principle keeps continuing. I am happy to hear that our hon. Minister Shri Piyush Goyal has mentioned that Jan Vishwas 3.0 is already under way. I think this is the sign of a healthy democracy where we keep evolving and keep looking at our past.

While these reforms at the Centre have eased compliance and built trust, we need to do so at the State also where we have a lot of interaction with citizens. In our State, some regrettably damaging laws like the Land Titling Act or the Three Capitals Act that the earlier Government tried to push through, have16.12.2025 1083 caused a lot of pain and confusion in citizens' minds, damaging trust. As soon as the NDA Government came to power in Andhra Pradesh, we provided clarity and have repealed these laws which have gone against the interests of citizens.

While these were in particular nefarious things, the overarching principle that repealing or revising the problematic laws that are creating conflict or laws that are outdated, is essential for bringing back transparency, trust, and predictability in governance. I look forward to aiding our State Government in continuing to do so.

The Repealing and Amending Bill, 2025 is not merely an exercise in removing obsolete statutes; it reaffirms our fundamental principle of good governance that laws which have outlived their purpose must be repealed with the same resolve with which progressive laws are enacted. This House bears the responsibility not only to legislate for the present, but to free future generations from needless regulatory bodies.

Hon. Chairperson, I thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak on this important Bill and I wish that the Government continues to do this to ensure that there is maximum governance, minimum government, empowering our citizens for a trust-based and efficient society.

SHRI KALYAN BANERJEE (SREERAMPUR): Hon. Chairperson, Sir, this is the Repealing and Amending Bil, 2025. Every year, we bring these types of Bills.

There is not much confusion about the Repealing and Amending Bill. There are some good parts which are corrected. One of them is regarding Speed Post.

Instead of Registered with AD, it will now be Speed Post with AD. It is good. It16.12.2025 1084 will be speedier. But I request one thing to hon. Law Minister. … (Interruptions) Hon. Law Minister, kindly see. So far as the caveat is concerned, the part which you have amended is that it has to be served upon the defendants or whatever the party. But a caveat is filed through the lawyer. Therefore, if you can put "the party and also the lawyer of the defendant", that will help; otherwise, it will be useless. If you want speedy justice, then my suggestion is that you add 'the lawyer of the defendant' or whatever the party where it is made through the lawyer only. There is no problem on that.

Sir, the problem is somewhere else. Now, we are amending the Act, we are bringing more and more Acts; but is speedy justice being delivered? Where are we stuck? I just give you one small example. When in the Supreme Court, filing of new cases was 40,000, the strength of the Supreme Court judges was increased to 34. In 2024, filing was more than 60,000. In 2025, till two days ago, filing was 70,000, but the strength of judges has not been increased. Computers and all that will not decide the fate of a case. A real judicial reform by increasing the strength of the judges is required. Unless it is done, nothing will be done in this country. So far as justice part is concerned, I am saying about it. We need more judges. VENKATESAN (MADURAI): Hon. Chairperson Madam, this Bill is aimed to repeal or amend more than 70 amendments. There is no second opinion on the fact that such obsolete acts are to be changed as per the changing times. These amendments are to be brought from making good as better and better as best. They should not rather bring amendments to make bad to worse and worse to worst. Our Hon Member Kalyan Banerjee talked about whatever is related to law department. Once a case is filed in the Judiciary, it may take at least one month for the case to come for hearing. After so many hearings, the judgment in that case may be pronounced after several years. This was clearly stated by Hon Member Shri Kalyan Banerjee. But our experience is totally opposite. Recently a case was filed in the Madurai Bench of Hon Madras High Court on 7th November 2025. This case was registered on 10 November 2025 and the judgement was pronounced on 1 December 2025. Within 20 days from the date of filing of a case, Judgement was pronounced. This issue is an old issue which was discussed by the Courts for centuries and Judgements were pronounced several times in the past as well. It is a curse that the mind-set of the Hon Judge is reflected through his Judgement. If the particular Judge has an opinion on this particular case, he should have transferred this case to a different Judge and kept himself out of controversy. I want to register in this august House that this much civilised nature was not visible in the Judiciary.

Similarly, our Hon MP Shri Kalanidhi Veerasamy quoted something stated by a  English translation of the speech originally delivered in Tamil.

former Judge of Hon Supreme Court. The Judge said that this law-making Body, the Parliament is unable to take time and discuss in detail before enacting a particular law. And as a result of this, the Judiciary and Courts face difficulties while making interpretations. Within 3 minutes, 4 labour codes were passed in this House without any discussion. We have passed a legislation affecting the lives of several Crores of labourers who are part of our 140 Crore population.

Earlier we got the feeling that the Judgements were pronounced as per the substantial arguments made in regard to the case. Now the Judgements are pronounced keeping in view the favours that they would be getting after retirement from the Post which they are holding. In such a fashion, Judgements are being pronounced as an entrance exam to the Post that would be occupied after the person's retirement. Friends I want to register here as a matter of concern.

I have been serving as Member of Parliament for the last 7 years. In all these 7 years I have seen that not even a single suggestion made by a MP from the Opposition has been included by the Government in the law. Not even a single suggestion or an amendment has been accepted by the ruling party. You objective is to bring a legislation and you do not have any slight inclination to uphold the democratic nature of this House which legislates laws controlling 140 Crore people of this country. Therefore, I strongly oppose this amendment Bill.

Thank you for this opportunity. Vanakkam.

SHRI BALYA MAMA SURESH GOPINATH MHATRE (BHIWANDI):

Honourable Chairperson Madam, I express my gratitude for giving me the opportunity to speak here today. Today, we are discussing the Repeal and Amendment Act, 2025. This act aims to repeal 71 outdated laws which includes 65 amended laws and 6 obsolete laws. Four laws are being amended: the General Clauses Act, the Code of Civil Procedure, the Indian Succession Act, and the Disaster Management Act. Since 2014, the Modi government has repealed or amended many old laws.

I will give you some examples where changes in the law are necessary but are not happening. There is the issue of renaming our new Navi Mumbai airport; the Maharashtra state government, through a unanimous resolution in the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council, proposed that it should be named after the late D.Y. Patil; but this proposal is pending for 3 years.

Therefore, there should be a law that ensures no oversight on such pending matters.

In our area, some private companies supply electricity, and due to privatization, many difficulties are arising. Therefore, there should be some law regarding this matter. Local people should be given priority in jobs and businesses in the state they reside in, and it is necessary to enact laws for this purpose. This should include the railway department, the revenue department, and other departments. There are many issues where it is necessary to give  English translation of the speech originally delivered in Marathi.

16.12.2025 1096

confidence to the people.

We form governments for the welfare of the people, but when making laws, we do not take them into confidence. Therefore, the government should pay attention to the needs of the local people through legal means.

On the Mumbai-Thane road, begging women and children are seen at traffic signals. Whether it is summer, monsoon, or winter, these children are seen naked. Police vehicles and government vehicles pass by, but no one pays attention. The issue of child abduction is serious across the country, and the government should pay attention to it.

Honourable Chairperson Madam, I support any appropriate changes that need to be made according to the time and changing circumstances. Thank you, for giving me the opportunity to speak.

SHRI SELVARAJ V. (NAGAPATTINAM): Hon Chairperson Madam, Vanakkam. Thank you for this opportunity. The laws that are proposed in this Repealing and Amending Bill 2025 consists of mainly the laws relating to the labour welfare, finance and banking, Universities and educational institutions. These have names in Hindi and Sanskrit.

There are agitations held against this act of the Government. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Indian Justice Code); Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (Indian Citizen Safety Code) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (Indian Evidence Act) are the three Criminal Acts passed in Parliament recently and assented to by Hon President of India. Ten Trade Unions have announced in  English translation of the speech originally delivered in Tamil.

one voice that nation-wide agitations are being held against the Four Labour Codes which were formed by abolishing 44 labour related Acts of the country.

In order to make changes to the Labour laws of the country, during the year 2020, Four Labour Codes were enacted. The trade Unions have strong opposed these Codes. And nation-wide strikes and agitations were held in this regard.

Particularly, in section 148A, in sub-section 2, words "Registered post, acknowledgement due" shall be substituted by "Speed post with registration and proof of delivery". In the Disaster Management Act of 2005, in Section 30 and Sub-section 2 and in Clause 6, 'Prevention' shall be substituted by the word 'Preparation'. I urge that these amendments are not to be made in a hurry.

Rather they should be discussed in detail before going for amendments.

Thank you for this opportunity. Vanakkam.

ADV. GOWAAL KAGADA PADAVI (NANDURBAR): Thank you, hon.

Chairperson Madam, for giving me this opportunity. I rise today to participate in the discussion on the Repealing and Amending Bill, 2025. On the face of it, the Bill appears technical, procedural and even harmless, but the Parliament is not a clerical office, and legislation is not a routine housekeeping exercise. Every repeal, every amendment, and every omission carries constitutional consequences, historical baggage and social impact. The House must therefore ask – and I do ask – why these laws are being repealed now, who benefits from these repeals, and whose rights may be invisibly diluted. The Bill is repealing certain central Acts, and amending the core procedural laws like the General Clauses Act, 1987; the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; the Indian Succession16.12.2025 1101 Act, 1925; and the Disaster Management Act, 2005. But history teaches us that the procedural changes often affect substantive rights, especially of the poor, tribals, women and the litigants who have limited access to justice.

Madam, there are important Supreme Court judgments that I want to narrate over here. The Supreme Court, in the case of Mohar Singh, held that the effect of repeal on accrued rights must be examined carefully; repeal does not automatically erase past rights unless explicitly stated. Similarly, in Kolhapur Canesugar Works Limited, the hon. Court had warned that savings clause cannot be mechanical and must be interpreted in favour of vested rights.

Madam, the Bill seeks to amend the CPC. It replaces 'registered post' with 'speed post with registration and proof of delivery'. The Supreme Court, in the case of Salem Advocate Bar Association had held that procedural law must serve justice, not obstruct it. The speed post infrastructure is uneven, especially in my tribal constituency Nandurbar, which is an aspirational district. Also, proof of delivery failures will result in ex-parte decrees, especially against the poor.

Not just that, it may lead to improper delivery of summons or notices that may cause harm.

There is an omission of Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act. The Supreme Court in Clarence Pais versus Union of India upheld the differential probate requirement, but observed that the legislature may revisit the colonial distinction if social conditions so demand. I want to ask the hon. Minister whether they are saying that the probate is not compulsory. I think this amounts to an appeasement politics on the basis of religion, which is being removed, and it is16.12.2025 1102 going to affect the family and the personal laws of all religions. I would urge the hon. Minister to kindly clarify this matter.

With respect to the Disaster Management Act, replacing 'prevention' with 'preparation' in Section 30 of the Disaster Management Act is not merely a cosmetic change. The Supreme Court in COVID-19 related judgement stressed that the State's duty is proactive prevention, not reactive preparation. Is the Government diluting its responsibility by shifting from preventive governance to post-disaster management?

I just want to ask one final question to the hon. Minister. For example, if you are bringing in the Repealing and Amending Bill, what about the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, िजसम(cid:164) (cid:250)ाम सभा का अिधकार था, वह छीन िलया गया?

You are taking away the powers and duties of a constitutional body and reducing it to a ceremonial body. जो फॉरे(cid:214)ट राइट अम(cid:164)डम(cid:164)ट ए(cid:179)ट था, जो (cid:250)ाम सभा को अिधकार देता था, अगर आपने वह छीन िलया, तो आप उसका अम(cid:164)डम(cid:164)ट कब लाएँगे? उससे आिदवासी लोग(cid:332) को सबसे (cid:186)यादा नुकसान हो रहा है ।

This Government repeatedly claims minimum Government, ease of doing business, legal simplification. But in reality, we witness maximum executive control, reduced parliamentary scrutiny and delegated legislation replacing debate. I urge the Government to refer this Bill to the Standing Committee on Law and Justice, table a rights impact statement for repealed laws, ensure explicit protection of pending cases, conduct district level feasibility studies on CPC amendments, clarify the safeguards following the omission of section 213 of the Indian Succession Act and reaffirm preventive responsibility under16.12.2025 1103 disaster management law.

Finally, I want to say that repealing a law is very easy, correcting historical injustice is hard, and protecting constitutional values is the hardest. Therefore, simplification must not become silent dilution, and efficiency must not replace equity. Governance must never override justice. That is all I want to say. Long live the Constitution.

SHRI MADDILA GURUMOORTHY (TIRUPATI): Thank you, Madam, for giving me an opportunity to speak on the Repealing and Amending Bill, 2025, which16.12.2025 1106 seeks to repeal outdated enactments and correct formal defects in existing laws.

If I quote a few positives in this Bill, they are as follows.

Clause 2 read with the First Schedule repeals obsolete enactments, ranging from the Indian Tramways Act, 1886 to several Amendment Acts passed between 2016 and 2023 that have already served their purpose. This exercise reduces legal clutter and improves statutory readability for citizens, businesses, and courts. Clause 4, the Savings Clause, is a critical safeguard. It protects accrued rights, liabilities, past actions, and pending proceedings, thereby ensuring legal continuity and constitutional certainty under Articles 21 and 300A.

Under the Second Schedule – General Clauses Act, 1897, Section 27, replacing "registered post" with "speed post with registration" aligns statutory language with modern postal systems and reduces procedural delays. Similarly, amendments to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, modernising service of summons through proof-of-delivery mechanisms, will improve dispute resolution timelines – an essential factor for ease of doing business, trade certainty, and cross-border commerce.

While the intent of the Bill is positive, certain concerns merit attention.

First, Clause 2 provides for a blanket repeal of multiple Amendment Acts without a consolidated restatement, which may create interpretational challenges for courts, lawyers, and administrators. Second, under the Second Schedule, procedural amendments are introduced without clear transition guidelines or capacity-building measures for subordinate courts and district administrations.

Without such support, the benefits of these reforms may not fully reach the16.12.2025 1107 ground.

I would like to seek some clarifications from the Government. First, Clause 2 read with the First Schedule: How will ambiguity be avoided in on-going litigation that relies on provisions contained in repealed Amendment Acts?

Second, Clause 3 read with the Second Schedule (Code of Civil Procedure, 1908): What steps will be taken to ensure uniform adoption of "proof of delivery" standards across all States? Third, Second Schedule – Indian Succession Act, 1925: Will uniform probate rules be notified to prevent divergent practices among High Courts?

Madam, I support this Bill. Thank you.

SABKA BIMA SABKI RAKSHA (AMENDMENT

OF INSURANCE LAWS) BILL, 2025

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE; AND MINISTER OF CORPORATE AFFAIRS

(SHRIMATI NIRMALA SITHARAMAN): Sir, I beg to move:

"That the Bill further to amend the Insurance Act, 1938, the Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956 and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999, be taken into consideration."

In the opening remarks, I would like to just highlight what the current ecosystem is. After all, the policy has moved towards reaching 100 per cent FDI  Moved with the recommendation of the President.

16.12.2025 1126

now. Earlier, we had amended it to reach 49 per cent. With that and many other changes, an ecosystem has developed in this country with greater access for people to insurance. The Insurance Ombudsman Rules were framed in 2017, and IRDAI was also established. They have established an elaborate framework for the protection of policyholders. The Government came up with several flagship programmes, like Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, and Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana. All these aimed at the poorest sections who can afford insurance but by keeping the premium less, we made access to insurance and as I said in the morning, that kind of access which came of help even during the big pandemic like Covid. Other than that, the Government also has been making sure that the public sector insurance companies can meet the insurance requirements of the people of India. So, by listing of LIC, for instance, we have made it transparent for people to know what is happening there and those who want to participate in the retail stock market, they can also come in. The GIC Re-insurance and New India Assurance are all in this direction.

Sir, with these kinds of steps taken, as I said, we moved from 26 per cent to 49 per cent in 2014-15, and then from 49 per cent to 74 per cent in 2021.

These have actually brought in greater push for the insurance sector. I will explain, how, by taking up some of the parameters. In 2014-15, the number of insurers were 53. Now, they are 74. Insurance penetration earlier was only 3.3 per cent. Today, it is closer to 3.75 or 3.8 per cent. Insurance density, that is, average insurance premium paid per person in a year is referred to when I say16.12.2025 1127 insurance density, it was 55 US dollars in 2014-15. Now, it is 97 US dollars. Total insurance premium in lakh crore rupees was Rs. 4.15 lakh crore in 2014-15.

Now, it is Rs. 11.93 lakh crore. Asset under management was Rs. 24.20 lakh crore in 2014-15. Now, it has gone up to Rs. 74.43 lakh crore.

FDI limit in insurance companies, as I said was raised from 49 per cent in 2014-15 to 74 per cent in 2024-25 whereas for insurance intermediaries, that 49 per cent which was the case in 2014-15 was made 100 per cent even in 2024- 25. So, with all these, now is the time when we are looking at greater penetration and we want to have the regulator also to be more robust and that is why, we have taken this in the amendment that we are bringing about. I am not getting into the details of each one of those but there will be a better regulatory oversight. There will be ease of compliance. Insurance intermediaries will provide uninterrupted services and we are also treating both intermediaries and insurance companies with a lot more standardized approach so that whenever they do anything, they will have to have a stakeholder consultation before they bring in any policy and so on. So, Sir, broadly, I will leave it here that it aims at bringing in transparency. There is a good need for insurance money and so an increase in FDI. Many compliance related issues are being eased out. There is, for instance, a legal requirement to seek prior approval. Even to seek approval of the IRDAI or the regulator for transfer of share capital, that is, even for one per cent, they will have to come and seek approval. But now, we are saying, no, you come only when it is five per cent so that there will be greater flexibility and so on. So, there are very many such measures. Once the discussion is over, I16.12.2025 1128 will take your permission and give the elaborate clarification and reply to all the Members.

So, with this, I look forward to having the debate.
